items.objective: Distinguish write intents, observed OS reads and prescribed application deliveries using byte intervals.
items.prompt: In the invented nine-byte capture, write intents are [0,3), [3,9); OS reads are [0,2), [2,3), [3,9); decoder deliveries are [0,1), [1,4), [4,9). Which claim follows from these recorded intervals?

choices.text: Delivery [1,4) contains bytes from both write intents; this capture does not guarantee the same OS reads on another run.
Delivery [1,4) must equal one OS read because the application gave it to the decoder in one call.
The sender made exactly two OS write calls and each became one message at the receiver.

feedback.a: Offsets 1 and 2 belong to the first intent, and offset 3 to the second. Grouping those three bytes is an application action; the read intervals describe only this capture.
feedback.b: No observed read interval equals [1,4). The application can retain bytes from reads and regroup them before a decoder call.
feedback.c: Write intents describe the write loop's intended ranges, not its OS call count. Messages require the framing rule; neither write count nor read count identifies them.

items.derivation: [1,4) intersects [0,3) in [1,3), length 2, and [3,9) in [3,4), length 1. The OS read intervals are independently supplied observations; no future-read premise is given.

items.objective: Complete an incremental frame trace when a delivery finishes two messages and starts another header.
items.prompt: Regroup the same toy stream 02 4f 4b 01 3f 03 52 55 4e into deliveries of 2, 4 and 3 bytes. After the SECOND delivery, what has that call returned and what remains pending? Toy lengths use one byte and allow 1..3.

choices.text: Return only OK; retain 01 3f 03 because one delivery can return at most one message.
Return OK and ?; retain 03, the next frame's header.
Return OK, ? and RUN; the final length byte proves the remaining letters are available.

feedback.a: After removing the completed OK frame, 01 3f is another complete frame. Continue the loop and consume it; otherwise a completed message is unnecessarily delayed.
feedback.b: The first two deliveries supply offsets [0,6). Frames [0,3) and [3,5) are complete; offset 5 is 03, whose three body bytes have not arrived.
feedback.c: A declared length does not supply the body. The second delivery ends at exclusive offset 6; RUN occupies offsets 6, 7 and 8 and arrives only in the third.

items.derivation: Delivery 1=[0,2): 02 4f, no complete frame. Delivery 2=[2,6): 4b 01 3f 03. Accumulated [0,6) consumes frame lengths 3+2=5, leaving 6-5=1 byte, 03. Returned payloads are OK and ?.

items.objective: Accumulate a split multi-byte header before decoding its length, then distinguish incomplete body from incomplete header.
items.prompt: Use a two-byte big-endian variant of the toy protocol, allowing lengths 1..4. A fresh decoder receives 00, then 02 41. After those two feeds, what is known?

choices.text: The first feed declared forbidden length 0, so it had to fail before the second header byte arrived.
The complete header declares length 2; one body byte A is present, so retain 00 02 41 and wait for one more body byte.
The second feed starts a new header 02 41, declaring length 577; previous pending bytes should be discarded.

feedback.a: One byte is insufficient for this two-byte header. Interpret a length only after both bytes arrive; a leading zero can be part of a valid length.
feedback.b: Combined bytes are 00 02 41. Header value is 0*256+2=2; the complete frame needs 2 header + 2 body = 4 bytes, and only 3 are available.
feedback.c: Feed boundaries do not restart framing. Preserve the pending 00 and combine it with the next 02; 41 then has the body role. Discarding pending bytes loses the stream position.

items.derivation: Header width=2. After first feed, available header bytes=1<2. After second, buffer=00 02 41, length=0*256+2=2, required total=2+2=4, available=3, deficit=1 body byte.

items.objective: Distinguish an empty feed from EOF and diagnose an incomplete suffix after earlier successful output.
items.prompt: Fresh application: feed toy bytes 01 58 03 59 5a. This returns X and retains 03 59 5a (length 3, only YZ present). Then call feed(b'') and finally finish(), with no further bytes. What should happen?

choices.text: The empty feed closes the stream successfully because it contains zero bytes.
finish succeeds because X was already emitted, so all later bytes may be ignored.
The empty feed emits nothing and leaves the suffix; finish refuses truncation because one body byte is missing.

feedback.a: Only finish announces EOF in this API. An empty feed adds zero bytes and cannot turn an incomplete open stream into a cleanly closed one.
feedback.b: Earlier output does not license dropping the suffix. X occupies its own complete two-byte frame; the second frame still requires three body bytes.
feedback.c: Pending has 1 header + 2 body bytes, while the promised frame needs 1+3=4. Empty feed adds none, so EOF arrives with a one-byte deficit. The earlier X remains an earlier valid event.

items.derivation: Input length=5. First frame length=1+1=2, leaving 3 bytes. Second required length=1+3=4, so deficit=4-3=1. feed(empty) adds 0; finish cannot accept a nonempty incomplete suffix.

items.objective: Reject a fully known invalid length without confusing it with an incomplete valid frame.
items.prompt: A fresh toy display decoder accepts lengths 1..3. Its first feed is the single byte 04, with no body. Which response follows from the protocol?

choices.text: Raise during feed: the complete header already declares 4, above the allowed maximum 3.
Wait for four body bytes, then decide whether the length was permitted.
Treat 04 as a body byte because the body has not yet arrived.

feedback.a: The toy header is one byte, so its value is fully known now. Since 4>3, no later body can make this frame valid.
feedback.b: Waiting is appropriate for an incomplete body under a permitted header. It is unnecessary once a complete header violates the length bound.
feedback.c: At the start of a fresh stream the first byte has the header role. Arrival timing cannot change that role into payload.

items.derivation: Header width=1, supplied bytes=1, declared length=0x04=4. Allowed interval is [1,3], and 4 is outside it. Refusal does not depend on body availability.

items.objective: Interpret cross-process observations without equating logging order or a measured gap with transport causality.
items.prompt: One saved trace records writer intent at 100 ns, a peer read at 130 ns, and the writer's write-loop return at 160 ns. All are relative observations from one host run. Which interpretation is supported?

choices.text: The peer caused the write, since its read was logged before the writer's return.
The read observation lies 30 ns after intent and 30 ns before return; scheduling and logging are included, so this is not an isolated transport-latency measurement.
Exactly 60 ns of network latency occurred, and the same gap must recur under the fixed delivery schedule.

feedback.a: A peer can receive bytes while the writer is still inside its loop or waiting to log return. Use byte order and each process's local sequence; return logging is not the creation of the bytes.
feedback.b: 130-100=30 and 160-130=30 describe the recorded observation gaps. They do not separate buffering, scheduling, code execution and logging from transport.
feedback.c: 160-100=60 is an intent-to-return observation span, not an isolated network quantity. This is a local pipe, and scripted application grouping does not fix scheduling or future timestamps.

items.derivation: Recorded gaps are 130-100=30 ns, 160-130=30 ns and 160-100=60 ns. The supplied data identify endpoints only; no premise isolates transport or requires repeatable timing.
